archetype.name: Improviser (turning Pocket Passer)
archetype.definition: A third-year passer who still holds the ball, extends plays and scrambles, but who now wins mostly with on-schedule accuracy from the pocket in Ben Johnson's offense rather than off-script magic.

report.headline: The accuracy leap is real; the recent interceptions are the thing to fix.
report.take:
Caleb Williams in 2026 is a different passer from the one in the career lines. In 2024 and 2025 he ranked in the bottom third for completion percentage and bad-throw rate, and his CPOE was negative both years. This season he is completing 68.3% with a 6.2 CPOE, 7th of 55 qualifiers. His bad-throw rate has fallen from 17.8% to 10.6%. His time to throw (3.16) and aggressiveness (11.0%) are almost identical to last year, so this is not a scheme that has turned him into a dink-and-dunk game manager. He is holding the ball as long and throwing into the same windows, and he is simply hitting them. That points to a real skill change, not a role change.

The efficiency has a clear shape. Close games are where he is best: 0.197 EPA per play within one score, and 0.32 in the red zone with 7 touchdowns and no interceptions. The intermediate and deep game produces the big plays (0.282 and 0.285 EPA per attempt) but also most of the turnovers, with 3 of his 6 picks coming on 10-19 yard throws. Rome Odunze is the engine downfield. His 0.659 EPA per target dwarfs every other regular, while Luther Burden and Kalif Raymond have been near-neutral on similar volume. Colston Loveland is the steady second option.

The red flag is the last three games: 5 interceptions, a 5.3% INT rate and EPA per dropback below zero (-0.021). Context softens it but doesn't erase it. Four of those picks came in one game against Tampa Bay, a top-3 defense by EPA. Seattle is top-6. The Saints game was a low-volume, 11.5-point-favorite grind. Across the season, 4 of his 6 interceptions came while leading by 9 or more, where his EPA per play is -0.227. That is a quarterback forcing throws when the game is already in hand, which costs less than it looks but is still a habit. Meanwhile his legs have quietly left the offense. Designed runs have been poor (-0.63 EPA), and his rushing has dropped to 9.3 yards a game over the last three.

Where it heads: the completion and bad-throw gains are the kind that stick, because they come with an unchanged process. The recent interception spike should settle back toward his season rate. That is no guarantee he returns to last year's low pick totals. His aggressiveness into the intermediate zone means a turnover-prone floor stays part of the package.

strengths.title: Real, process-backed accuracy jump
strengths.body: His CPOE swung from deeply negative to top-10 in the league. The bad-throw rate fell sharply even though time to throw and aggressiveness didn't move, so he isn't buying completions by throwing safer balls. That is the most sustainable kind of improvement, a mechanical or processing gain, and it should hold.

strengths.title: Best when the game is tight
strengths.body: Within one score he has produced 0.197 EPA per play, and in the red zone 0.32 EPA with 7 touchdowns and no interceptions. His fourth-quarter-close CPOE is 12. Red-zone numbers on 34 plays will cool, but the close-game efficiency rests on a large sample and is the real version of him.

strengths.title: Scrambles still pay
strengths.body: The improviser in him survives in a useful form. He scrambles on 7.9% of dropbacks at 0.546 EPA per scramble, and half of them move the chains. Those extended plays are why his long time to throw is a trade worth making. His pressure-to-sack rate has stayed far from the 2024 version's bottom-of-the-league mark.

concerns.title: Interceptions when playing with a lead
concerns.body: Four of his six interceptions have come while leading by 9 or more, where his EPA per play falls to -0.227. That reads as forcing aggressive throws when the game no longer demands them, not as a coverage-reading failure in high-leverage spots. It's fixable and costs fewer wins than raw INT counts suggest, but it is now a pattern rather than a one-off.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws carry the risk
concerns.body: The 10-19 yard window is his biggest EPA source per attempt, but it comes with only a 50% completion rate and 3 interceptions. That is the cost of the aggressiveness that makes him dangerous, so it won't disappear. It will keep his INT rate above league average even in good weeks.

concerns.title: Fading rushing contribution
concerns.body: Designed runs have been a losing play (-0.63 EPA, 62.5% stuffed), and his rushing has fallen to under 10 yards a game over the last three. Much of his early rushing production came from a two-touchdown opener. Without the legs, his weekly floor leans more on passing touchdowns.

trend.note: His passing EPA has slid game by game since the Week 7 high against New England, bottoming out with the four-interception day against Tampa Bay and a flat outing against New Orleans. Two of those three opponents now rank top-6 on defense, so the slide is partly schedule, but the turnovers are his.

nextGame.headline: A leaky Lions secondary in a 55.5-point indoor shootout
nextGame.body:
Detroit is the kind of opponent that flatters this version of Williams. The Lions rank 26th in pass defense EPA and 27th against short throws. They allow quarterbacks 20.7 PPR points and 2.3 touchdowns a game, both near the bottom of the league. Opponents also pass against them far more than usual. Their own offense ranks 4th in EPA, which points to the game the Book's 55.5 total predicts: a dome shootout where the Bears can't sit on a lead. That also keeps him out of the comfortable-lead situations where his interceptions have piled up. The catch is Detroit's pass rush, 5th in hit rate and 4th in sack rate, against a quarterback with a 3.16-second time to throw.

Availability tilts his way. Safety Chuck Clark (91% of snaps) missed Monday's walkthrough with a hamstring, and corner Ennis Rakestraw is out. Edge/linebacker DJ Wonnum and DT Skyler Gill-Howard are questionable, which could thin that pass rush. On his side, right-side tackle Theo Benedet (75% of snaps) is questionable with a quad. On a four-day turnaround against a good rush, his absence would matter more than usual. His own old practice designation is stale; he has played every snap since Week 6.

keyMatchups.title: Loveland against a TE-friendly defense
keyMatchups.body: Detroit has been the second-worst defense in the league against tight ends, by both PPR points over average and EPA per target. Tight ends draw a bigger share of targets against them than the league norm. With Clark possibly out at safety, the middle of the field should open for Loveland, his second-most-targeted receiver.

keyMatchups.title: Lions rush vs. his long clock
keyMatchups.body: Detroit gets home: 5th in hit rate, 4th in sack rate. Chicago's line has been among the best at keeping him clean, but Benedet's status and the short week test that. If he holds the ball looking for Odunze downfield, this is where sacks and hurried throws come from.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script
keyMatchups.body: The Book's 55.5 total and Detroit's 3rd-ranked pass offense suggest Chicago will need to keep throwing all game. That should mean more volume and fewer of the comfortable-lead snaps where his EPA has gone negative.

nextGame.watch: Whether he takes the easy short and middle throws Detroit concedes or keeps forcing intermediate balls. His interception count decides if this is a big day or a messy one.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the accuracy to hold. A top-10 CPOE built on a sharply lower bad-throw rate, with the same time to throw and aggressiveness, is the most durable change in his profile. With Odunze producing at a rate no other target matches, his yards per attempt should stay well above league average. The Bears' 7th-ranked defense will keep handing him leads, though, and a slightly run-leaning offense in those spots caps his volume in blowouts. Somewhere around 240 to 285 passing yards a game with 1.4 to 2.0 touchdowns is the realistic band.

The interception spike of the last three games should cool, since one four-pick game against a top-3 defense drives much of it. Still, his intermediate aggression and the leading-by-two-scores habit mean 0.6 to 1.0 picks a game is the honest range, not last year's lower rate. His rushing is the piece likely to stay muted. Designed runs aren't working, so his legs show up mainly as scrambles, worth roughly 10 to 25 yards a game.
swingFactors: Cutting the forced throws with a lead
Pass protection if Benedet misses time

confidence.note: Seven starts, but the accuracy gain is backed by a changed bad-throw rate; turnover rate is the noisy part.
